name: Filter Methods Benchmark for Feature Selection
description: The amount of data for machine learning (ML) applications is constantly growing. Not only the number of observations, especially the number of measured variables (features) increases with ongoing digitization. Selecting the most appropriate features for predictive modeling is an important lever for the success of ML applications in business and research. Feature selection methods (FSM) that are independent of a certain ML algorithm - so-called filter methods - have been numerously suggested, but little guidance for researchers and quantitative modelers exists to choose appropriate approaches for typical ML problems. This review synthesizes the substantial literature on feature selection benchmarking and evaluates the performance of 58 methods in the widely used R environment. For concrete guidance, we consider four typical dataset scenarios that are challenging for ML models (noisy, redundant, imbalanced data and cases with more features than observations). Drawing on the experience of earlier benchmarks, which have considered much fewer FSMs, we compare the performance of the methods according to four criteria (predictive performance, number of relevant features selected, stability of the feature sets and runtime). We found methods relying on the random forest approach, the double input symmetrical relevance filter (DISR) and the joint impurity filter (JIM) were well-performing candidate methods for the given dataset scenarios.
general_score_metric: predictive_performance (classification accuracy) along with stability and number_of_selected_features
reputation: Well-regarded review and empirical benchmark in the feature-selection literature; commonly cited by researchers comparing classical filter methods.
notes: Non-LLM benchmark focused on classical ML filter methods; reports multiple criteria (accuracy, stability, selected feature count, runtime), so results should be interpreted per-criterion and per-scenario; may not directly transfer to deep-learning feature representations.
